Pregnancy

Nub theory: what an early ultrasound can and cannot tell you

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

An early ultrasound can prompt plenty of guesses about a baby’s sex. Nub theory has a basis in developing anatomy, but the reliability of a prediction depends on timing, the actual view and who is interpreting it.

What people mean by nub theory

Nub theory is a popular name for estimating fetal sex from the angle of the genital tubercle on an early ultrasound image. The genital tubercle is a small developing structure in the genital area. Early in pregnancy, external genital structures look similar before their development becomes more distinguishable.

The method is usually discussed around eleven to thirteen weeks, sometimes extending into the fourteenth week. It is an interpretation of a particular ultrasound view, not a change that parents can reliably see from the outside or work out from pregnancy symptoms.

Curiosity is understandable, especially while waiting for a later scan. However, the label “theory” can blur two different things: a trained examiner making an assessment under defined conditions, and someone drawing lines on a shared still image. They do not have the same evidence or reliability. An early guess should stay a guess unless the clinical team explains otherwise.

The angle is measured against the fetal body

Descriptions commonly compare the tubercle with a reference line along the lower spine or nearby skin surface in a true side-on, midsagittal view. A tubercle pointing clearly upward at more than about thirty degrees has been used as a male prediction in research. A more parallel or downward orientation has been used as a female prediction.

Online guides often describe a low angle of around ten degrees or less as female and a ten-to-thirty-degree interval as uncertain. Those cut-offs are not a universal standard across studies. For example, the 1999 Efrat study used a different low-angle convention. A picture with a line added to it is not automatically applying the same method as a published investigation.

The relevant comparison is with the baby’s anatomy, not the horizontal edge of the photograph. Rotating the image on a phone does not correct an unsuitable scan plane. Nor can measuring an angle more precisely rescue a picture that does not clearly show the structures needed for the assessment.

A usable image is more than a clear-looking photograph

The position of the fetus, the view obtained and the examiner’s experience all affect whether an assessment is possible. A curled or moving fetus may not provide a suitable reference line. The structure being labelled also has to be the genital tubercle rather than an adjacent feature.

A sonographer can examine a moving sequence, adjust the probe and decide that a prediction should not be made. A printed image or cropped screenshot captures only one moment. It may have been selected to record the head, body length or another measurement, not to show the genital region.

“Unable to tell” is therefore a useful result, not a failure that needs an internet second guess. Before comparing opinions, ask whether the original image was intended for this assessment and whether the clinician considered it adequate. Several confident comments based on the same unsuitable picture do not provide independent confirmation.

Accuracy changes with gestational age

Early genital development is a major reason that a prediction made at eleven weeks may be less dependable than one made later. The baby’s size and the quality of the view matter alongside the week written on the image. “Twelve weeks” is not a guarantee that every scan has equal information.

In a 1999 study of 172 singleton pregnancies examined before chorionic villus sampling, reported accuracy rose from 70.3% at eleven weeks to 98.7% at twelve and 100% at thirteen. These were results from that selected study, not promises for all pregnancies, all operators or photographs posted online.

That study also found more early male fetuses were assigned female than the reverse, with errors falling at later gestations. It does not establish a universal rule that a particular early female prediction will change. Different studies use different methods and populations, so combining attractive percentages from several sources into a personal accuracy chart is misleading.

Check what an accuracy percentage actually counts

A study can report accuracy only among scans where an examiner was willing to predict, or success across all the scans attempted. Those denominators answer different questions. Excluding images that could not be interpreted can make a method sound more dependable for an everyday appointment than it really is.

In one routine-practice study, first-trimester success was 75% overall and 91% when scans without a prediction were excluded. Results also varied with fetal age and the individual sonographer. This illustrates why a single “over ninety percent” headline leaves out information a family needs.

Ask who made the assessments, at what gestation, how many could not be assigned and how the eventual result was confirmed. A research paper showing that a technique can work under some conditions does not validate every commercial service using its name. Confidence expressed by the person making a prediction is not itself a measure of accuracy.

How it differs from folklore and pregnancy symptoms

Nub assessment has an anatomical basis that can be studied using ultrasound and later confirmation. It is different from predictions based on a Chinese calendar, a swinging ring, cabbage-water colour changes, cravings or the shape of a bump. These household methods should not guide medical decisions.

That distinction does not make an online nub guess certain. There is a spectrum between an unsupported tradition and a carefully performed clinical assessment. The important questions are whether the required image is available and whether the interpretation has appropriate limits.

If guessing is enjoyable, keep it separate from a medical result and avoid making irreversible plans around it. If it brings pressure, conflict or disappointment, it is reasonable to stop asking for predictions. Parents can choose to know later, or not to know before birth at all, without changing the care their pregnancy deserves.

What later scans and blood tests can tell you

A mid-pregnancy anatomy scan, commonly around eighteen to twenty-two weeks depending on the service, may show external genital anatomy more clearly. Its main purpose is to assess development. The view, local policy and your preference affect whether sex is discussed, and ultrasound is not a one-hundred-percent guarantee.

Some non-invasive prenatal testing panels can provide information related to sex chromosomes from cell-free DNA in a maternal blood sample. Much of the pregnancy-related DNA comes from the placenta. Routine NIPT is a screening test for specified chromosome conditions, with limitations; it is not a complete genetic diagnosis or a universal confirmation of every aspect of sex development.

Specialist non-invasive prenatal diagnosis is a separate pathway used for selected conditions, including some pregnancies at risk of sex-linked disease. If a genetic condition is the reason for asking about fetal sex, a genetics or fetal-medicine team should select and interpret the test. An early ultrasound guess must not determine whether clinically indicated testing is accepted or declined.

Use the result with clear expectations

At the next appointment, ask what the scan was designed to assess, whether a sex prediction was actually made and how uncertain it is. If two results disagree, take both reports to the clinical team rather than deciding that one online angle measurement settles the issue.

Tests and scans examine particular anatomical or chromosomal features. They do not predict a child’s future gender identity, personality or preferences. Keeping those distinctions clear makes conversations about the result more accurate and less loaded with expectations.

You can enjoy wondering about your baby while leaving room for uncertainty. A useful plan is to record an early prediction as provisional, continue the recommended pregnancy assessments and decide beforehand whether you want any later information disclosed. The quality of antenatal care does not depend on obtaining the earliest possible answer.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Angle conventions and accuracy figures differ between studies.

A clear still photograph may not provide the correct view for a prediction.

Clinical decisions about sex-linked conditions need an appropriate specialist testing pathway.

How BeMama can help

Ask whether your scan included a formal prediction and how uncertain it is; keep online guesses separate from the clinical report.

When to seek help

Do not use nub theory to make decisions about prenatal genetic testing or treatment. Discuss discordant results or an inherited-condition risk with your maternity or genetics team.

Sources and further reading

  • Efrat and colleagues, Ultrasound in Obstetrics & Gynecology — First-trimester determination of fetal gender by ultrasound
  • Kearin and colleagues, Australasian Journal of Ultrasound in Medicine — Accuracy of sonographic fetal gender determination: predictions made by sonographers during routine obstetric ultrasound scans
  • NHS — Ultrasound scans in pregnancy
  • NHS Genomics Education — Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT)
  • NHS Genomics Education — Non-invasive prenatal diagnosis (NIPD)

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Early genital structures can look similar.
  • The angle is relative to fetal anatomy, not the photograph’s border.
  • Study percentages are not individual guarantees.
  • NIPT and specialist NIPD are different tests with different purposes.
  • You can choose whether to receive information about fetal sex.

Frequently asked questions

What is the nub?

It is the developing genital tubercle, a small structure examined in some early ultrasound assessments.

Does an upward angle prove the baby is male?

No. An upward angle is one research criterion, but an adequate view, timing and expert interpretation are needed and errors occur.

What does an angle between ten and thirty degrees mean?

Some online guides call it uncertain. Angle thresholds vary, and this range should not be treated as a universal diagnostic rule.

Can I use the edge of the scan photograph as the baseline?

No. The reference relates to the fetus’s lower spine or nearby skin surface, not the edge of the image.

Is nub theory 100% accurate at thirteen weeks?

No. A study reporting 100% in one selected group does not guarantee that result in other scans or in an individual pregnancy.

Why do different websites quote different percentages?

They may use different studies, gestations, operators and denominators, including whether unassignable scans were excluded.

Is this the same as a ring or calendar prediction?

No. Nub assessment has an anatomical basis, but that does not validate an online interpretation of an unsuitable image.

Will the anatomy scan always reveal sex?

No. The position, image quality, local policy and your preference affect whether it can or will be discussed.

Is all blood testing for fetal sex the same?

No. Routine NIPT screening and specialist NIPD for selected medical questions have different purposes and limitations.

Should an early guess change testing for a sex-linked condition?

No. A genetics or fetal-medicine team should guide the appropriate testing and interpret its results.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
